title: Ground Effect

intro.en: Rev 1 — narration from the recording, cleaned ("swelling the air" → swirling the air, "lifttoff" → lift-off, "high tail tail / tatail" → high tail / T-tail, "EOA" → AoA, "PTO" → Pt (total/pitot pressure), "P_T_S" → Pt − Ps, "full sense of performance" → false sense of performance, "goaround" → go-around, "highwing" → high-wing). Before teaching: (1) page 7 is wrong about wing position: the slide says high-wing aircraft "experience more pronounced ground effect" and low-wing aircraft "a weaker ground effect". The strength of ground effect depends on the wing's height above the ground relative to its span — a LOW wing is closer to the surface, so it enters ground effect earlier in the flare and feels it more strongly. High-wing trainers "float" mainly because they are flown fast in the flare, not because the high wing gives a stronger cushion. Fleet: C172S and T206H = high wing; DA42 HS-NAS = low wing with T-tail; (2) add the numbers: ground effect starts at about one wingspan; at a height of 1/4 span induced drag is reduced by about 24 %, at 1/10 span by about 48 % (FAA PHAK); (3) add the pitch effect: on a conventional (low) tail, reduced downwash at the tail increases the tailplane's angle of attack, giving a nose-down pitching tendency in ground effect — more back pressure needed in the flare; on leaving ground effect after take-off the opposite, a nose-up tendency; (4) the ASI/static-pressure page is consistent with standard texts (entering ground effect: higher static pressure → ASI and altimeter under-read; leaving: ASI may over-read), but the size of the error is aircraft-specific (POH — SME); (5) the soft-field take-off technique in the C172S POH deliberately uses ground effect: lift off early, level off in ground effect, accelerate to Vx/Vy, then climb (POH — confirm, SME); (6) page 10 landing panel ends with the static-pressure text ("These pressure changes can significantly impact instrument readings…") — copy/paste error; (7) Kabinburi runway length, surface and local float/landing-distance factors — SME.

pages.t: Ground effect and its impacts on aviation
pages.on: Title text and overview; wing-in-ground-effect craft over water.
pages.en: Ground effect is an aerodynamic phenomenon every pilot meets during take-off and landing, even if it is not always noticed straight away. It occurs when an aircraft flies very close to the ground — typically within about one wingspan — and the airflow around the wing changes in a way that improves performance. As the wing gets closer to the surface, the ground interferes with the normal formation of the wing-tip vortices. They become smaller and weaker, which reduces the downwash behind the wing. With less downwash the wing becomes more aerodynamically efficient, and induced drag drops. At the same time the airflow becomes more parallel to the ground, creating a kind of cushioning effect under the wing. The combined result is important: for the same angle of attack, lift increases and drag decreases near the ground. That sounds like a benefit, and it is, but it also creates operational challenges. Ground effect can make an aircraft lift off earlier than expected or float longer during landing, so pilots must anticipate it and manage speed, attitude and technique carefully.

pages.t: Ground effect: a cushion of air
pages.on: Normal flight (vortices fully developed, strong downwash, induced drag) vs ground effect (ground interference, reduced downwash, significantly reduced induced drag); real-world example; simple takeaway.
pages.en: Ground effect is like the aircraft flying on a thin cushion of air when it gets very close to the runway. It does not mean the wing suddenly becomes more powerful, but it does mean the wing becomes more efficient for a short moment. Normally, when a wing produces lift, some air from the high-pressure area under the wing curls around the tip into the low-pressure area on top. That creates wing-tip vortices, and those vortices create downwash behind the wing. Downwash is basically the wing pushing air downward, and that costs energy; the energy loss shows up as induced drag. When the aircraft is close to the ground, the ground gets in the way of that airflow. The tip vortices cannot fully develop, so they become smaller and weaker. With weaker vortices, downwash reduces and the wing does not waste as much energy swirling the air. As a result, induced drag drops significantly. Because induced drag is lower, the aircraft needs less power to maintain the same speed, and it can generate more lift at the same angle of attack. This is why during landing the aircraft often feels as if it wants to keep flying and floats just above the runway. During take-off it can lift off a little early and then feel stuck close to the ground until it accelerates enough to climb normally. So the simple takeaway is: near the ground the wing becomes more efficient, and you feel that as extra lift and reduced drag, which affects how the aircraft behaves in the flare and just after lift-off.

pages.on: 1 Height threshold — within one wingspan above the ground (B747 graphic); 2 speed and angle factors — low speed, high angle of attack at take-off and landing.
pages.en: Ground effect has two key characteristics that help you predict when you will feel it and how strong it will be. One, the height threshold — within one wingspan. Ground effect becomes noticeable when the aircraft is very close to the ground, typically within about one wingspan above the surface. The closer you get, especially in the last few metres before touchdown, the stronger it becomes, because the ground interrupts the normal airflow around the wing, weakening the tip vortices and reducing induced drag. So the runway is not just a place to land — it actually changes the aerodynamics of the wing when you are near it. Two, it is stronger at low speed and high angle of attack. Ground effect feels most powerful when the aircraft is slow and at a higher angle of attack, because that is exactly when induced drag is normally at its highest. During take-off and landing the wing is working hard to produce lift at low speed, so weakening the vortices makes a noticeable difference. That is why on landing the aircraft may float longer in the flare: you reduce power, but the wing still feels efficient, so it does not settle as quickly as expected. On take-off the aircraft may lift off early and then feel as if it is hovering close to the runway until you accelerate — it can fly in ground effect at a lower speed than it needs to climb safely out of it. So in practice ground effect is strongest close to the runway, at slow speed, with the wing at a higher angle of attack — exactly the conditions of the most critical phases of flight.

pages.on: B747 take-off photo; 1 premature lift-off risk; 2 control challenges; 3 pilot awareness; key takeaway.
pages.en: Ground effect can make a take-off feel easier than it really is, and that is why pilots need to treat it with respect. Premature lift-off happens because close to the runway induced drag is reduced and the wing becomes more efficient. The aircraft may start flying and lift off even though it has not yet reached the proper speed for a safe climb. From the cockpit this can feel like a normal rotation because the aeroplane does become airborne, but it is often only flying well because ground effect is helping it. The problem shows up as soon as you try to climb out of ground effect. Once the aircraft rises higher, the tip vortices return to normal strength, induced drag increases and the wing needs more airspeed to maintain lift efficiently. If the aircraft is still below the required climb speed, it may feel sluggish, struggle to climb, or begin to settle back toward the runway. That is the control and performance trap: the aeroplane was comfortable in ground effect, but it was not truly ready to climb away. This is why pilot awareness and discipline are essential. The correct technique is to avoid rotating too aggressively or too early and to make sure the aircraft accelerates to a safe speed before climbing out. If you do lift off early, the safest strategy is usually to stay in ground effect, hold a shallow attitude, let the aircraft accelerate to the correct speed, and then transition to a normal climb once you have the energy margin. In simple terms: ground effect can get you airborne, but airspeed is what lets you climb away safely.

pages.on: Four steps: 1 approach (increased lift), 2 floating, 3 touchdown (flare timing), 4 roll-out (extended distance); summary.
pages.en: On landing, ground effect is one of the main reasons an aircraft can feel as if it does not want to settle onto the runway. One, approach: as you descend through the last part of the approach very close to the surface, the aircraft enters ground effect. Induced drag reduces and the wing becomes more efficient, so for the same pitch and power the aircraft may produce slightly more lift than expected. This can reduce your sink rate and make the aircraft feel as if it is cushioning just above the runway. Two, floating: during the flare that extra efficiency often causes float. Instead of touching down where you expect, the aircraft keeps flying in ground effect while slowly bleeding off speed. If the approach speed is even slightly high, the float becomes more noticeable and the aircraft can travel a long way down the runway before it settles. Three, touchdown: to manage this, time the flare carefully and avoid holding off too long. The goal is a controlled reduction in descent rate while the aircraft decelerates smoothly to touch down without excessive float. Precise speed control on final is critical, because extra airspeed means extra lift, and ground effect makes that lift last longer. Four, roll-out: because float increases the touchdown distance, it reduces the runway remaining for braking. A long float can lead to a longer landing distance overall, needing firmer braking, better energy management, or sometimes a go-around if the touchdown point is no longer acceptable. In short, ground effect turns small speed errors into big landing-distance changes, so accurate approach speed and disciplined touchdown aiming are the keys to safe landings.
pages.th: ในการลงจอด ground effect เป็นเหตุผลหลักอย่างหนึ่งที่เครื่องรู้สึกเหมือนไม่อยากแตะทางวิ่ง ข้อหนึ่ง approach เมื่อร่อนลงผ่านช่วงสุดท้ายของ approach ใกล้พื้นมาก เครื่องเข้าสู่ ground effect แรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำลดลงและปีกมีประสิทธิภาพมากขึ้น ที่ pitch และกำลังเท่าเดิม เครื่องอาจสร้างแรงยกมากกว่าที่คาดเล็กน้อย ทำให้อัตราจมลดลงและรู้สึกเหมือนมีเบาะรองอยู่เหนือทางวิ่ง ข้อสอง การลอยตัว ในช่วง flare ประสิทธิภาพที่เพิ่มขึ้นมักทำให้ลอย แทนที่จะแตะพื้นตรงที่คาด เครื่องยังบินอยู่ใน ground effect ขณะความเร็วค่อย ๆ ลดลง ถ้าความเร็ว approach สูงไปเพียงเล็กน้อย การลอยจะชัดขึ้นและเครื่องอาจไปได้ไกลตามทางวิ่งก่อนจะแตะพื้น ข้อสาม การแตะพื้น ต้องจับจังหวะ flare อย่างระมัดระวังและไม่ hold off นานเกินไป เป้าหมายคือลดอัตราจมอย่างควบคุมได้ ขณะให้เครื่องชะลอความเร็วอย่างนุ่มนวลและแตะพื้นโดยไม่ลอยมากเกินไป การควบคุมความเร็วบน final อย่างแม่นยำสำคัญมาก เพราะความเร็วเกินหมายถึงแรงยกเกิน และ ground effect ทำให้แรงยกนั้นอยู่นานขึ้น ข้อสี่ การวิ่งลงจอด เพราะการลอยทำให้ระยะถึงจุดแตะพื้นยาวขึ้น ทางวิ่งที่เหลือสำหรับเบรกจึงลดลง การลอยนานอาจทำให้ระยะลงจอดรวมยาวขึ้น ต้องเบรกแรงขึ้น จัดการพลังงานดีขึ้น หรือบางครั้งต้อง go-around ถ้าจุดแตะพื้นรับไม่ได้แล้ว สรุปคือ ground effect เปลี่ยนความเร็วที่ผิดเล็กน้อยให้กลายเป็นระยะลงจอดที่เปลี่ยนไปมาก การคุมความเร็ว approach ให้แม่นและการเล็งจุดแตะพื้นอย่างมีวินัยจึงเป็นกุญแจของการลงจอดที่ปลอดภัย

pages.on: High-wing aircraft ("experience more pronounced ground effect… stronger air cushion, increased lift, better stability", Cessna); low-wing aircraft ("generally experience a weaker ground effect", Piper); design considerations; key takeaway.
pages.en: Wing position changes how strongly ground effect is felt, because it changes how close the wing — and its downwash and vortices — is to the surface. Low-wing aircraft: the wing is physically closer to the ground, so it enters ground effect higher up the flare and the effect is stronger in the last moments before touchdown. Airflow around the wing is also influenced by the landing gear and flaps, and pilots often describe the result as a pronounced cushion that makes the aircraft sensitive to excess speed and pitch changes, depending on the type. High-wing aircraft: the wing is farther above the ground during the flare and early lift-off, so for the same span the ground effect is weaker and comes later. High-wing trainers are still often described as "floaty" close to the runway, but that is mostly because of excess approach speed and their gentle handling — the reduced induced drag near the surface makes any extra speed last longer. Design considerations: designers consider this because ground effect influences rotation behaviour, flare and float, and landing distance. A design that floats more may feel comfortable and forgiving, but it can need more runway when speed control is poor; a design that settles more predictably makes touchdown control easier but may feel less forgiving in the flare. In practice the biggest factor is still airspeed control: a fast approach will float in any aircraft, while wing position changes how strongly and how early you feel ground effect in the final few feet.

pages.on: High tail (T-tail): above the disturbed airflow, more stability; low tail (conventional): more susceptible to ground-effect influences; design trade-offs; key takeaway.
pages.en: Tail configuration affects how an aircraft feels in ground effect, because the tailplane works inside the flow field created by the wing and the ground. High tail, or T-tail: the horizontal stabiliser sits above much of the disturbed airflow close to the runway, so it is more likely to see a cleaner, more consistent relative wind. Pitch control and trim then feel more predictable in the flare, because the tail stays out of the strongest downwash changes near the surface, and a high tail can help keep the pitch response steady as the aircraft moves into ground effect. Low tail, or conventional tail: a low tail is more directly exposed to changes in the wing's downwash and to the ground-modified flow behind the wing. Ground effect reduces the downwash and changes the local relative wind at the tailplane; that increases the tailplane's angle of attack, reduces the tail download and gives a nose-down pitching tendency, so pilots notice a change in pitch feel and the way the aircraft settles in the flare. In some designs this can also change the flare timing and the amount of float. Design trade-offs: engineers choose tail position by balancing much more than ground effect — stability and control, clean airflow versus wing-wake influence, drag and efficiency, and structure and weight (a high tail needs a stronger fin). There are operational risks too, such as a deep-stall tendency on some T-tail aircraft at very high angle of attack. The simple takeaway: a high tail tends to stay in cleaner airflow and feel more consistent near the ground, while a low tail is more affected by the changing downwash in ground effect, which can subtly change pitch response during landing.
pages.th: รูปแบบหางมีผลต่อความรู้สึกของเครื่องใน ground effect เพราะแพนหางทำงานอยู่ในสนามการไหลที่ปีกและพื้นสร้างขึ้น หางสูงหรือหางแบบ T แพนหางระดับอยู่เหนือการไหลที่ถูกรบกวนส่วนใหญ่ใกล้ทางวิ่ง จึงมีแนวโน้มเห็นลมสัมพัทธ์ที่สะอาดและสม่ำเสมอกว่า การควบคุม pitch และ trim จึงคาดเดาได้มากกว่าใน flare เพราะหางอยู่พ้นการเปลี่ยนแปลงของ downwash ที่แรงที่สุดใกล้พื้น หางสูงช่วยให้การตอบสนองทาง pitch คงที่ขณะเครื่องเข้าสู่ ground effect หางต่ำหรือหางแบบธรรมดา หางต่ำได้รับผลโดยตรงจากการเปลี่ยนแปลงของ downwash ของปีก และจากการไหลหลังปีกที่ถูกพื้นปรับเปลี่ยน ground effect ลด downwash และเปลี่ยนลมสัมพัทธ์ที่แพนหาง ทำให้มุมปะทะของแพนหางเพิ่ม แรงกดลงของหางลดลง และเกิดแนวโน้มหัวทิ่มลง นักบินจึงสังเกตการเปลี่ยนความรู้สึกทาง pitch และวิธีที่เครื่องจมลงในช่วง flare บางแบบอาจเปลี่ยนจังหวะ flare และปริมาณการลอยด้วย ข้อแลกเปลี่ยนในการออกแบบ วิศวกรเลือกตำแหน่งหางโดยชั่งหลายเรื่องมากกว่า ground effect ทั้งเสถียรภาพและการควบคุม การไหลที่สะอาดเทียบกับอิทธิพลของ wake ปีก แรงต้านและประสิทธิภาพ และโครงสร้างกับน้ำหนัก (หางสูงต้องใช้แพนหางดิ่งที่แข็งแรงกว่า) ยังมีความเสี่ยงในการปฏิบัติ เช่นแนวโน้ม deep stall ของเครื่องหาง T บางแบบที่มุมปะทะสูงมาก สรุปง่าย ๆ คือ หางสูงมักอยู่ในการไหลที่สะอาดกว่าและรู้สึกสม่ำเสมอกว่าใกล้พื้น ส่วนหางต่ำได้รับผลจาก downwash ที่เปลี่ยนไปใน ground effect มากกว่า ซึ่งอาจเปลี่ยนการตอบสนองทาง pitch เล็กน้อยระหว่างลงจอด

pages.t: Static pressure measurements in ground effect
pages.on: 1 entering ground effect: increased static pressure → ASI under-reads; 2 in ground effect: altered pressure field; 3 leaving ground effect: decreased static pressure → ASI over-reads; "static pressure explained" box.
pages.en: When an aircraft gets very close to the ground, the airflow and pressure field around the fuselage change, and that can slightly disturb the static pressure sensed at the static port. Because the airspeed indicator works by comparing pitot (total) pressure with static pressure, even a small static-pressure error creates an IAS error — especially during take-off and landing, when you are low and slow. One, entering ground effect, the ASI may under-read. As you descend into ground effect, the pressure distribution around the aircraft can increase the local static pressure at the static port. If the port senses slightly higher static pressure than the true ambient pressure, the difference Pt − Ps becomes smaller, so the ASI shows less airspeed than you actually have. Two, in ground effect, static pressure is distorted. While you remain in ground effect the airflow is more horizontal and downwash is reduced, so the static pressure around the fuselage may not match the undisturbed atmosphere and IAS can be slightly inaccurate. The size of the effect depends on the aircraft type, the port location and the exact height above the surface. Three, leaving ground effect, the ASI may over-read. As you climb out of ground effect, the static-pressure effect reduces and may swing the other way. If the port now senses slightly lower static pressure than ambient, Pt − Ps becomes larger, and the ASI can momentarily read higher than actual. Why should pilots care? These effects are usually small, but they happen at the most critical moments — rotation, lift-off, flare and touchdown. The best protection is to fly correct technique and reference speeds, cross-check pitch attitude and performance, and avoid chasing tiny IAS fluctuations close to the ground.

pages.t: Pilot awareness during take-off and landing
pages.on: Take-off: maintain proper take-off speed, resist premature rotation, monitor performance, be prepared for sudden lift increase. Landing: approach speed, descent rate, flare timing, touchdown point. Landing text box repeats the static-pressure text.
pages.en: Pilot awareness during take-off. During take-off, ground effect can give you a false sense of performance, so the key is to stay disciplined and fly the numbers, not the feeling. First, maintain the proper take-off speed. As the aircraft accelerates you want a healthy, continuous build-up of airspeed. The aeroplane may feel light on the wheels earlier than expected, but that does not mean it is ready to climb safely: ground effect temporarily reduces induced drag and increases lift, so the aircraft may unstick before it has enough energy for a stable climb. That is why you must resist premature rotation. If you rotate too early, the aircraft can lift off and stay a few feet above the runway, but as soon as you try to climb out of ground effect the wing has to work harder again — vortices strengthen, induced drag increases and performance drops. The aircraft may feel sluggish, struggle to climb, or even settle back toward the runway. So after lift-off, monitor performance carefully: confirm that the aircraft is still accelerating and responding normally. If the climb is weak or the speed is not building, the safest technique is often to remain in ground effect — stay low and let the aircraft accelerate to a safe climb speed before committing to a full climb. Finally, be ready for the aircraft to feel different as it leaves ground effect: the cushion disappears, drag increases, and it may need more power and correct pitch control to maintain the climb. A smooth, patient take-off built on correct speed and technique keeps the departure safe. Pilot awareness during landing. On landing, ground effect is most noticeable in the last few feet above the runway, and it shows up as floating, especially if you carry extra speed. It starts with approach-speed control: if you come in even slightly fast, you bring extra energy into the flare, and when you enter ground effect the wing becomes more efficient, so the aircraft does not lose speed and lift as quickly as you expect. The result is a longer float and a touchdown further down the runway. That is why you must manage the descent rate carefully. A stable approach with a controlled descent is the best set-up; if the aircraft is too flat, too fast, or you reduce power too early, you can end up skimming above the runway waiting for it to settle. Next is flare timing and technique: in ground effect the aircraft can feel as if it wants to keep flying. Your flare needs to be smooth and controlled enough to reduce the sink rate, but not so much that you hold the aircraft off excessively. The goal is to touch down at the correct attitude and the correct speed, not to keep it floating. Finally, always protect the touchdown zone. Know where the aircraft must touch down; if you float past that point and the landing no longer feels assured, the safest decision is to go around. Ground effect can make a landing feel gentle, but it can also quietly consume runway, so discipline, speed control and firm touchdown planning are essential.

pages.en: Ground effect feels subtle, but it has a real influence on performance whenever the aircraft is flying just a few feet above the surface. As the wing gets close to the ground, the tip vortices weaken, downwash reduces and induced drag drops. The wing becomes more efficient, so the aircraft can produce more lift with less drag than it would at the same speed higher up. During take-off this efficiency boost can tempt the aircraft to lift off early, or make it feel ready to climb before it actually has enough airspeed. The critical point is that ground effect may help you become airborne, but you still need proper speed to climb away safely. If the aircraft lifts off too soon, the best practice is to stay low in ground effect, build airspeed and then transition to a normal climb. During landing, ground effect usually shows up as floating. As the aircraft enters ground effect in the flare it loses lift more slowly, so it can stay airborne longer and touch down further down the runway, especially if the approach speed is high. That is why accurate approach-speed control, smooth flare timing and protecting the touchdown zone are essential. Overall, ground effect does not change the laws of aerodynamics — it changes the efficiency of the wing near the ground. Understanding it helps pilots manage take-off and landing energy correctly, helps engineers predict handling, and improves safety by reducing surprises during the most critical phases of flight.
pages.th: ground effect รู้สึกได้อย่างแผ่วเบา แต่มีอิทธิพลจริงต่อสมรรถนะทุกครั้งที่เครื่องบินอยู่เหนือพื้นเพียงไม่กี่ฟุต เมื่อปีกเข้าใกล้พื้น tip vortex อ่อนลง downwash ลดลง และแรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำลดลง ปีกมีประสิทธิภาพมากขึ้น เครื่องจึงสร้างแรงยกได้มากขึ้นด้วยแรงต้านที่น้อยลงเมื่อเทียบกับความเร็วเดียวกันที่สูงขึ้นไป ระหว่างวิ่งขึ้น ประสิทธิภาพที่เพิ่มขึ้นนี้อาจล่อให้เครื่องยกตัวเร็ว หรือทำให้รู้สึกพร้อมไต่ก่อนจะมีความเร็วพอจริง ประเด็นสำคัญคือ ground effect อาจช่วยให้ลอยขึ้นได้ แต่ยังต้องมีความเร็วที่ถูกต้องเพื่อไต่ออกไปอย่างปลอดภัย ถ้าเครื่องยกตัวเร็วเกินไป แนวปฏิบัติที่ดีที่สุดคืออยู่ต่ำใน ground effect สร้างความเร็ว แล้วจึงเปลี่ยนเป็นการไต่ปกติ ระหว่างลงจอด ground effect มักแสดงออกเป็นการลอย เมื่อเครื่องเข้า ground effect ใน flare จะเสียแรงยกช้าลง จึงลอยอยู่ได้นานขึ้นและแตะพื้นไกลออกไปตามทางวิ่ง โดยเฉพาะถ้าความเร็ว approach สูง นี่คือเหตุผลที่การคุมความเร็ว approach ให้แม่นยำ จังหวะ flare ที่นุ่มนวล และการปกป้อง touchdown zone จึงจำเป็น โดยรวม ground effect ไม่ได้เปลี่ยนกฎของอากาศพลศาสตร์ แต่เปลี่ยนประสิทธิภาพของปีกเมื่อใกล้พื้น การเข้าใจเรื่องนี้ช่วยให้นักบินจัดการพลังงานในการขึ้นและลงได้ถูกต้อง ช่วยให้วิศวกรทำนายการบังคับได้ และเพิ่มความปลอดภัยด้วยการลดความประหลาดใจในช่วงการบินที่วิกฤตที่สุด

numbers: Ground effect starts at ≈ 1 wingspan; strong below ≈ ½ span.
Induced drag reduction (FAA PHAK): ≈ 24 % at ¼ span, ≈ 48 % at 1/10 span height.
Span (type data — SME): C172S/T206H ≈ 36 ft (high wing); DA42 ≈ 44 ft / 13.4 m (low wing, T-tail).
Entering ground effect: same α → more CL; conventional tail → nose-down tendency; static pressure ↑ → ASI and altimeter under-read. Leaving: reverse (nose-up, ASI may over-read).
Low wing feels ground effect more strongly and earlier than high wing (closer to the surface).
C172S (POH — confirm, SME): rotate ≈ 55 KIAS, Vx ≈ 62 KIAS, Vy ≈ 74 KIAS, short-field approach 61 KIAS full flap.
Excess approach speed → float → longer landing distance; no touchdown in the planned zone → go around.
corr: High-wing aircraft "experience more pronounced ground effect"; low-wing "generally experience a weaker ground effect".
Reversed: ground effect depends on wing height/span — a low wing is closer to the ground and feels it more strongly and earlier.
Direction of the pitch change not stated.
Conventional tail: reduced downwash at the tail → nose-down tendency entering ground effect (nose-up on leaving).
No figures for the size of the effect.
Added FAA PHAK figures: −24 % induced drag at ¼ span, −48 % at 1/10 span.
